name: Akai MPC3000
originalPurpose: The successor to the MPC60 and the last Akai MPC Roger Linn designed: stereo sixteen-bit sampling, a resonant filter, and the same pad-and-sequencer workflow.
whatActuallyHappened: In Detroit, J Dilla made it the instrument of a new sense of time. Instead of letting the machine snap each hit onto the grid, he left the timing as he played it, with the kicks and snares landing slightly early or late. His own unit, a limited edition from 2000, is now in the collection of the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.
priceStory: No launch price is sourced here. It sold as a professional studio tool, like the MPC60 before it.
hook: The sampler J Dilla used to make drums sound slightly drunk on purpose, which changed how a generation of musicians thought about time.
blurb: The MPC3000 came out in 1994. Like the MPC60 it had sixteen pads, but it recorded sound more clearly and had a filter that could make sounds darker or brighter. It matters here less for what it could do than as the instrument on which J Dilla worked out another way to handle time. Machines like this have a setting, quantise, that fixes your timing by moving every drum hit exactly onto the beat, and by then most people used it without thinking. Those around Dilla describe him mostly working with it off. His drums land a little early or a little late, and the beat seems to lean and stumble while still grooving, a feel that spread from his productions into live drumming and neo-soul. His own MPC3000 is now kept by the Smithsonian. Neither its launch price nor when it stopped being made is sourced here, so the map shows its end as unknown.
